comparison.title: Acoustic and optical phonons compared
comparison.note: Both are quanta of lattice vibration, not molecules; optical phonons also involve atomic displacement. The phase and centre-of-mass descriptions below apply to the long-wavelength limit of this diatomic chain.
comparison.mediumA: Require interacting atoms in a lattice.
comparison.mediumO: Also require a lattice; they are not photons propagating in vacuum.
comparison.motionA: The two atoms in each cell move approximately in phase, in the same direction.
comparison.motionO: The two atoms move out of phase; both still undergo displacement.
comparison.centerA: Moves with the long-wavelength vibration; this does not imply continuous material transport.
comparison.centerO: At Γ, mA uA + mB uB = 0: the centre of mass stays fixed while both atoms vibrate.
comparison.frequencyA: Tends to zero; the exact Γ zero mode is a rigid translation.
comparison.energyA: Vibrations have kinetic and potential energy; atoms move near equilibrium.
comparison.energyO: Also have kinetic and potential energy; a stationary centre of mass does not mean stationary atoms.
modes.branches: A primitive cell with n atoms in a 3D crystal has 3n displacement degrees of freedom: 3 acoustic and 3n−3 optical branches.
modes.oneDimension: Only longitudinal motion is included here: 2 atoms × 1 degree of freedom = 2 branches, one acoustic and one optical. A branch describes frequency as a function of wave vector.

modes.sublattices: Sublattices A and B are the two sets of atomic sites obtained by repeating each labelled position under lattice translations. Each cell in this model contains one A atom of mass m and one B atom of mass 2m. A and B do not denote electric charges. Circles and diamonds distinguish the two sets of sites.

cells.title: Unit cells and supercells: from repetition to a calculation model
cells.unit: A unit cell tiles the crystal through lattice translations. Lattice vectors define those translations; the atomic positions within a cell describe the basis.
cells.primitive: A primitive cell has the smallest volume and contains one lattice point, but may contain several atoms. One lattice point does not necessarily mean one atom.
cells.conventional: A conventional cell is often larger to display symmetry. Monatomic BCC and FCC conventional cubic cells contain 2 and 4 atoms respectively, while their primitive cells each contain 1. Ideal monatomic HCP has 2 atoms per primitive cell; the full hexagonal prism above is not the smallest cell.
cells.superTitle: A supercell is a larger periodic repeat unit
cells.super: Repeating a chosen cell builds a supercell. A 2 × 2 × 2 supercell contains 8 starting cells and, without adding or removing atoms, 8 times as many atoms. The starting cell can be primitive or conventional.
cells.matrix: These equations describe integer scaling along three directions. More generally, an integer matrix S combines lattice vectors, with volume ratio |det S|. A supercell still repeats under periodic boundary conditions.
cells.disorder: Represent larger local environments: assign species, dopants or defects to different sites to approximate chemical disorder. A finite supercell still repeats periodically; it is not an infinitely random material.
cells.forces: Finite-displacement phonons: displace atoms, calculate forces on the supercell atoms, and obtain force constants. The cell must be large enough to capture the relevant interaction range.
cells.cost: Balance accuracy and cost: larger supercells generally cost more. Check size convergence and interactions with periodic images; simply enlarging the cell does not guarantee correctness.
reciprocal.title: Where does reciprocal space come from?
reciprocal.intro: Real space describes where atoms are. Reciprocal space uses wave vectors to describe how rapidly and in which direction a pattern varies. It represents spatial information through waves and Fourier components, rather than another space containing atoms.
reciprocal.wave: Vibrations, electronic waves and periodic densities can be analysed using plane-wave components. The wave vector specifies the direction of phase variation; its magnitude is inversely proportional to wavelength. One wavelength corresponds to a phase change of 2π.
reciprocal.units: We use the physics convention including 2π: positions in Å give wave vectors in Å⁻¹. Wave-vector space is continuous; reciprocal lattice points are the discrete points compatible with lattice periodicity.
reciprocal.period: For any lattice translation R, the plane wave has the same phase at r and r + R when G·R is an integer multiple of 2π. The vectors G satisfying every lattice translation form the reciprocal lattice.
reciprocal.indices: aᵢ are real-space basis vectors and bⱼ are reciprocal basis vectors. δᵢⱼ equals 1 for i = j and 0 otherwise. h, k, l and m are integers; scalar k here is an integer coefficient, not the wave vector.
reciprocal.build: Each cross product is perpendicular to the other two real-space basis vectors. Dividing by the signed primitive-cell volume ensures aᵢ·bⱼ = 2πδᵢⱼ, including for non-orthogonal lattices.
reciprocal.bz: The first Brillouin zone is the region closest to the reciprocal-space origin: the reciprocal lattice Wigner–Seitz cell. k and k + G have the same Bloch phase under lattice translations, so inequivalent wave vectors are usually labelled within the first zone.
reciprocal.demoTitle: 1D example: a larger real-space period gives a smaller reciprocal period
reciprocal.demoNote: This example uses a monatomic chain: N primitive cells of spacing a form a supercell. Blue marks one supercell. Below, compare primitive-cell and supercell first Brillouin zones.
reciprocal.inverse: In 1D, reciprocal lattice spacing is 2π/a. A supercell of length L = Na has reciprocal spacing 2π/L. For N = 1 the two are identical.
reciprocal.uphoTitle: How does reciprocal space connect to UPHO?
reciprocal.use: Phonon dispersion ω(k) groups frequencies into branches at each wave vector. Reciprocal space analyses vibrations by spatial period and direction and provides paths for comparing materials.
reciprocal.fold: The smaller supercell Brillouin zone folds several primitive-cell k points onto one supercell K, making the branches appear denser. Merely repeating an ideal crystal creates no new physical vibrations; changing species or defects changes the physical model.
reciprocal.unfold: UPHO projects supercell modes onto the translation symmetry of an ideal reference primitive cell and displays their weights at primitive-cell wave vectors. GSC is a supercell reciprocal vector. Unfolding helps compare spectra; it does not automatically rank materials or guarantee cheaper upstream calculations.

waveGuide.title: A map of wave vectors: Γ and the Brillouin zone
waveGuide.intro: Γ, X and L label wave-vector positions in reciprocal space, not destinations for atoms inside a material. Selecting q specifies how vibration phases vary between cells. A Brillouin zone is a region; Γ is one point within it.
waveGuide.q: The direction of q gives the direction of phase variation; its magnitude determines wavelength. A lattice translation R changes the Bloch phase by q·R. Here a is the repeat length of an A/B cell, while neighboring A and B atoms are a/2 apart. Adjacent cells differ in phase by qa.
waveGuide.bzTitle: First Brillouin zone: distinct wave vectors
waveGuide.bz: The first Brillouin zone is the region closest to the reciprocal-space origin. A 1D lattice has reciprocal spacing 2π/a, giving −π/a ≤ q ≤ π/a, with equivalent endpoints. q and q + G, where G is a reciprocal lattice vector, have the same lattice-translation phase.
waveGuide.gamma: Γ is the zone center. Corresponding atoms in every cell share a phase, but A and B within a cell need not move in phase: the acoustic Γ mode is a zero-frequency rigid translation, while the optical Γ mode can have opposite A/B motion. Wavelength diverges as q approaches zero.
waveGuide.edge: At a 1D zone edge, adjacent cells differ in phase by ±π: corresponding atoms have opposite vibration signs, and the wavelength is 2a. This is an intercell relation; the relative amplitudes and phases of A/B within a cell still depend on the selected mode.
waveGuide.path: 1D first Brillouin zone and the selected q
waveGuide.slider: The pale region is the full first zone. The green segment is the Γ → π/a path sampled by the slider below; the orange dot follows its value. Positive and negative q have equal frequencies in this model, so half the zone suffices to illustrate frequencies.
waveGuide.current: Selected position and phase difference between adjacent cells:
waveGuide.symmetryTitle: What about X, L, M and K?
waveGuide.symmetry: These label high-symmetry points in 2D or 3D reciprocal space. Their positions depend on lattice type and coordinate convention; not every zone edge is X. A dispersion path such as Γ–X–L samples frequencies along specified segments, concatenated on the plot axis. It is neither an atomic trajectory nor a map of the entire zone. This 1D example labels its edge π/a without calling it X.
